questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to understand the American mindset and why they choose to elect Trump as president.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was very hard to find people who were both informed and Trump Supporters. My peer students were very young and seemed rather immature. I don't regret the trip, but the payoff was not as great as I had expected. I was also not able to get the courses I would ideally get so I will be set back a bit but that was within my expectations.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I was fortunate that I didn't need a lot of information. Once I was in, I had no issues with finding course material, maps and assistance from faculty.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got a student ID and advice for what classes would fit my criteria..

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation was set a the 5th of January. I was not able to attend until the 9th so I missed out on most of it. From what I gather, the orientation was not especially helpful with the most important aspect being a tour of the campus.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I joined multiple facebook pages for housing in the city and refreshed often, I found a place that was very cheap and close by. However, the flatmates had no idea of this so they were not expecting me, they happened to not be very welcoming and the apartment was rather low quality. I paid around 900 plus utilities each month. The apartment was not at all insulated from sound or temperature. There was mold in the bathroom and I had my bike stolen from the property. The apartment would also shake but that was not a big issue. I was located next to 3 fraternities which held parties that were exclusive to women and friends of the frat. There was a straight 20 minute walk to the university ad 12 minutes to the nearest busstop. I always felt safe. The alternative is to get a proper apartment which a lot of my peers did, its more expensive but might be worth it. But it takes a long time to get into one. (I didn't have much time).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There are lots of frats that are noisy. There are also a lot of homeless people. There are no discount chains in the city so you would have to go a long way to get to a good supermarket which is hard without a car but you can take a bus pretty directly, (busses are free with student id's)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing wasn't the worst but it could easily have been better circumstances.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No issues and they were the most helpful staff I met.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to wait until I was in America and I could only choose subjects a few days before I started. I was also a second priority for choosing courses to the continuing students. The university also only offered one class for a course i needed and It was full. I had to take two minor subjects which are set on the initial level but I choose two subjects that I have had nothing to do with so that was to my benefit. My major subject (economics) were rather limited, most of the courses are very low level with their "4th year requirements" classes seemingly being below my second year classes. They have a more fluid system of taking classes, I could drop my classes and add new ones until 6 weeks into the semester without any issue.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had to call to get permission to join the "harder classes" to make sure I had the correct prerequisites, they took my word for it and made it very easy to qualify.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: The one class I needed was full and despite being on a wait list, I never got it. there were some other courses that I would have liked but ultimately, I had few choices for more advanced econ classes which resulted in me having 3 days were I had a 8am module in something I wasn't very interested in. I could have chosen less advanced courses with better times but I choose to take a more advanced courses (for no reason)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It can not be expected that you will be offered the course you need. I regret not taking a graduate class, (they would have required them to consider my transcripts and at the time, I thought it wouldn't be worth it) all classes are really easy. There is also often weekly handins that take a little time but are useless (multiple choice questions from a book, a journal entry and preparation for discussion for the class) all have very low expectations but still take some time, you need to have done 95% of them or they will affect your grade, I think you should skip a few, you will likely get good grades anyways, (I got two As and two Bs doing only the minimum requirement).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some fun classes but it seemed mostly a waste of time. Only one class had attendance so I would highly recommend just not showing up and seeing the exchange as a holiday rather than anything else.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Very low level. Things I learn in Gymnasium (highschool) seemed new to them, my classemates were graduating the same as me (they would be 2-3 years younger than me) and they did not know the terms I would use. Most often, they did not take the classes because they wanted the degree but as prerequisites for something else (medicin and law). They need almost entirely As so they are expected to do work as anything below an B will be seen as soft failing the class and then no longer being able to compete with their classmates for jobs. In this way, the difficulty could be seen as hard but there is very little technical skills involved (we had not calculus or programming and tests were often multiple choice with very little free written questions.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is similar in that the professor will teach us something and we will get given assignments about the subject.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Public Economics, Health and Society, Intro to Chinese History and Environmental Economics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Intro to Chinese History. This was the only subject where I learnt completely new stuff that I would actually find interesting. It went trough Chinese history. it was not very practical as we didn't really talk much about sources in the later dates but there was a lot of critical thinking of discussing how the following people might want to portray the previous regime as being corrupt etc. In the Economy classes, the theory was the exact same as stuff I learnt in my first year (Økonomiske principper A&B) but with different names, I found very little of it to be new or useful.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went to the dentist and paid 3000 kr for a checkup... Food is also very variable, it is very expected that students eat out while I mostly made food at home. Expect the price to be much higher, you will also need to have a car or have it delivered, delivery is free when using more than 95 USD at a time.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Clothes were less expensive. Everything seemed very similar to the danish prices without vat, so around 20% cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs and orgs. I was however not picked for any orgs, (I rushed two frats, one I didnt like, the other one didnt like I was only there for a semester and thought I was too old, (they want people who are more malleable) and the orgs also didnt like that I was only there for a semester) I did join 3 clubs that turned out to be pretty great.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Most sports, and lots of hobbies. There were also multiples of certain actives like different band options and football (soccer)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The running club is a good community, I also personally like Meow mates and Model united nations, many of my friends also played soccer. People are however typically much younger and less experienced in drinking. I would also recommend attending the theater guilds productions, they are free for UT students and rather well made.  I think it is a good idea to spread a wide net first and find out which clubs have people you like. There is less "club activity" than I would have expected.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would highly encourage anyone on exchange to ditch the classes and go on extended holidays to see stuff. It is slightly more expensive, but my best experiences have been renting a car and driving out to places to see. Gas was really cheap. It is rather hard to maintain a good drinking habit. Frats will have open parties where guys pay 20-40 usd to enter and will have free jungle juice but there I was very underwhelmed by this, it feels a lot more transactional. There are practically no clubs where I was.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, no large changes, younger people but they were all mostly educated and left wing. But there is real segregation. People very largely stay with their own races. Frats are largely white and Latin American, theater was entirely white. Meow mates was Asian dominated. Soccer was Latin dominated. etc.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk about their interests, I found it is usually a good idea to talk about what you like about America, they will almost always like to talk about that or about good things about their club, the uni etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Tipping, 15% is the minimum for shit service, 25% is excellent service for food, tipping is for when you sit down and food is given to you, dont tip if you get your own food. for services, either a fixed amount (5 usd) or 20% is expected. Secondly, Americans are rather bad at discussing things. They are rather polarized, if you say something they disagree with, they will avoid you. I did probe them but quite a few people said that a violent revolution was necessary and if ICE would come to their communities to harm them. They would fight back, I said that seemed escalator and could further risk harming either themselves or their communities, this seemed to have made the shun me, they would ask if i sympathized with the Nazis which I took as a joke which might have given them the wrong impression. They just don't seem very "open" towards different perspectives. They seem unable to relate to other peoples and cant always explain their opinions.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are very open, they will talk to you and ask about you. I don't know know if I thought it was a good or bad thing, but people spend a lot, houses there are rather big and with lawns and plenty of people have really nice cars, they also eat out daily and get deliveries.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: buy earplugs, get Amazon prime subscription (Free 6 months for university students). Find a core friend group and try to be the active one so you can get stuff done.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You often don't have to be in the club to have the clubmembers as friends. join as many clubs early and get some friends you can relate to and stick to them. There are sometimes weekly events open for everyone (Friday board games or something similar) but you will get bored if you don't go out and actively do things. Most things also cost money but they can be fairly cheap, get a friend with a car and drive to an arcade, pay 13 USD to get in and 6 usd for fountain drinks and you can spend the rest of the day there drinking all the fountain drink you could want.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I got some good friends and memories, I went on a roadtrip up california, that was amazing and I would go again for that.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I was bored a lot of the time, especially in the beginning. I didn't find I needed much time for homework but I didn't have any close friends that could take me places. I felt stuck a lot of the time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I think UT might be a bit mundane, it isn't very different, I would recommend going to a more exciting place like Houston or a different state. You do need a car to get to most interesting places, going shopping takes an hour by bus each way. The weather was almost always wonderful (30 degree sunshine)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
